title: Effect of Strong Field Space-time Features on Vacuum Pair
authors: B. An, N. S. Lin, C. K. Li, M. Jiang, Y. J. Li
abstract: The relativistic dynamics of bound states across inertial reference frames are investigated using the computational quantum field theory (CQFT). The results reveal that the spatiotemporal properties of bound states within a given potential well are strictly frame-dependent. Crucially, this spatiotemporal modulation of the external field enables a reduction in the laser intensity threshold required for vacuum electron-positron pair creation. Analytical and numerical calculations demonstrate that this threshold reduction originates from the Lorentz transformation of the four-momentum, which reshapes the vacuum excitation pathways in phase space. By developing CQFT, we establish a comprehensive framework in which relativistic effects intrinsically govern the quantum vacuum decay process
summary: This paper uses Computational Quantum Field Theory (CQFT) to study electron-positron pair creation induced by strong, time-varying electromagnetic fields. The core finding is that the relativistic motion of the field source modifies vacuum physics, significantly lowering the required laser intensity threshold for pair production. By analyzing frame dependence via Lorentz transformations, the authors establish a comprehensive framework linking spacetime geometry directly to quantum vacuum decay.
main_problem: The study investigates how strong, time-dependent space-time features affect the vacuum pair production rate of electron-positron pairs.
main_result: The spatiotemporal modulation provided by a relativistically moving potential well significantly reduces the laser intensity threshold required for pair creation. This reduction is fundamentally linked to the Lorentz transformation of four-momentum, reshaping vacuum excitation pathways in phase space.
method: The research employs Computational Quantum Field Theory (CQFT) alongside semi-analytical methods like the Instantaneous Resonance Field Method (IRFM). These techniques are used to solve the time-dependent Dirac equation for pair production probabilities.
model_or_system: The system models electron-positron pair creation in a strong external field, specifically using a potential well $V(z, t)$ that moves relativistically. The dynamics are governed by the Dirac equation, and comparisons are made between results obtained in the laboratory frame and a moving reference frame via Lorentz transformations.
key_observables: Total number of created pairs ($N_{e}, N_{p}$), tunneling probability ($\langle E_p | 	ext{En} angle^2$), momentum spectra of positrons ($P_z$), and the energy Full Width at Half Maximum (FWHM) of bound states.
important_parameters: Laser intensity, relative velocity ($v_0$), Lorentz factor ($\gamma$), and characteristic potential parameters ($V_0, D, W$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the observed pair creation enhancement is due to relativistic phase-space reconfiguration governed by Lorentz transformations, rather than just increased field strength.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the time evolution of pair numbers for rest vs. relativistic motion in both frames; they also show momentum spectra and tunneling probabilities derived from bound state analysis across different reference frames.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the CQFT framework to model pair creation in a moving potential well. It then compares results between the Lab frame and the Relativistic frame using Lorentz transformations, analyzing how bound state properties (energies, FWHM) transform, culminating in the conclusion about threshold reduction.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it applies advanced quantum field theory techniques to understand non-perturbative QED phenomena. The explicit focus on relativistic kinematics and frame dependence provides a deep insight into how spacetime geometry influences fundamental vacuum processes, which has parallels in analyzing extreme astrophysical environments or high-energy particle collisions.
